sentences.text: She went out at the same time every evening for a fortnight and the eel was always in a pool on the street, and never the same pool.
That was the whole of the phenomenon and it does not sound like much written down.
Vera would like to insist that it did not feel like not-much at the time.
She started marking.

She used stones at first and then, when she worked out that people kicked stones, she used a stick to draw a line in the crust from pool to pool, and she extended it each evening from wherever the eel was.
The rule she gave herself, which she took extremely seriously, was that she was only allowed to draw as far as the eel had been.
Not as far as she could see the low ground going.
As far as the eel had actually been on an evening she had witnessed.
She has thought since that this was the only genuinely good decision she made that summer, and that she made it for no reason at all except that it felt like cheating otherwise.
By the end of the fortnight she had a line four hundred metres long, and it did not go where she expected.
She had assumed the road went from the dam road to the church, because that is the way people were walking.
It did not.

It came in from the north, along the flank of the slope, and made a wide turn about a hundred metres out that took it well away from the tower and then brought it back — a proper turn, the kind you make for a gradient, not for a boundary.
And it did not end at the church.

It went past the church, on the north side, and there was a second line going off it at right angles that she found on the eleventh evening and that ran forty metres and stopped at a rectangle of stone about the size of a kitchen.
She drew all of it in a notebook, with the tower as the fixed point, pacing distances and writing them down.
She showed nobody for three weeks, because it was hers.
She did tell one person, on the second Saturday, which was a boy from the caravan site called Diogo who was there for a fortnight and who she thought would be interested.
He came out with her once, looked at a line drawn in mud, said it was cool, and asked whether there was anything to actually see.
She said no, not really, and he was perfectly nice about it, and they went back and played cards.
That was the last time she told anybody until September.
She told her grandmother in the middle of September, in the kitchen, on an evening when the rain had finally started and everybody knew the pools were going.
She did not lead up to it.
She put the notebook on the table and said, "This is the road into the village." Her grandmother wiped her hands and sat down and pulled it towards her, and looked at it for a long time.
Then she put one finger on the wide turn.
"That's wrong," she said.
